questions.question: What are ActiveRecord associations and how do you declare them?
questions.title: ActiveRecord Associations Basics
questions.direct_answer: Active Record associations declare relationships between model classes and provide methods for navigating and changing related records. In a one-to-many relationship, `Post has_many :comments` and `Comment belongs_to :post`; the foreign key normally lives on the belonging table as `comments.post_id`. The Ruby declarations do not replace database design: migrations should add the reference, index, null rule, and foreign key needed for integrity, and destructive dependency behaviour such as `dependent: :destroy` must be chosen explicitly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the common macros (belongs_to/has_many/has_one), what foreign key they rely on, and the convenience methods they give you.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the foreign key convention (post_id) or confusing which side has belongs_to vs has_many.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: belongs_to/has_many/has_one declare model links; they rely on foreign keys and give you post.comments and comment.post for free.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `belongs_to` is declared on the model whose table holds the foreign key.
- `has_many` exposes the collection on the other side of a one-to-many relation.
- Associations add methods such as `post.comments` and `comment.post`.
- A migration still supplies the column, index, nullability, and foreign key.
- Choose `dependent` behaviour deliberately; it controls related rows on deletion.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An Active Record association describes how two model classes are related and gives Ruby methods for using that relationship. The relationship still rests on database columns. In a one-to-many example, one `Post` has many comments, and every `Comment` stores the post it belongs to.

Declare `has_many :comments` on `Post` and `belongs_to :post` on `Comment`. The foreign key belongs on the comments table as `post_id`, because each comment points to one post. The model declarations tell Rails how to navigate; they do not create the column themselves.

Rails then provides `post.comments`, `comment.post`, and collection builders such as `post.comments.build(body: "Clear")`. Building through the collection fills the relationship in memory; saving still runs the child's validations and write lifecycle. The association collection can also be filtered or ordered before it loads.

A migration should add the reference, index, null rule, and foreign-key constraint required by the domain. Choose `dependent: :destroy` only when child records truly belong to the parent's lifecycle, because it destroys them and runs callbacks. Audit records may instead need deletion restricted or their ownership preserved.

sections.title: The object graph sits on top of foreign-key rows
sections.content:
An association method starts from key metadata. `comment.post` uses the comment's `post_id` to find the matching post primary key. `post.comments` builds the inverse condition. The returned collection is an association relation, so it can often be filtered or ordered before loading.

Building through an association sets linkage in memory. `post.comments.build` assigns the post relationship to the new comment; persistence still runs the comment's validation and write lifecycle. Creating the child does not automatically make a multi-record operation atomic, so transactions matter when several writes must succeed together.

Database foreign keys protect references even when SQL, background jobs, or another service writes outside the Rails model. An index on the foreign-key column supports the lookup direction. Model-level presence rules improve feedback but cannot replace those database guarantees.

Dependency options encode ownership. If comments have no meaning without their post, destroying them may be correct. If records must remain for audit, cascade deletion may be destructive. Model behaviour and database `ON DELETE` actions must be designed together so they do not contradict or unexpectedly duplicate work.

sections.title: Complete Rails example: declare, migrate, and build the relation
sections.content:
```ruby
class Post < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy
end

class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :post
end

class AddPostToComments < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.1]
  def change
    add_reference :comments, :post,
                  null: false, index: true, foreign_key: true
  end
end

post = Post.new
comment = post.comments.build(body: "Clear explanation")
puts comment.post.equal?(post)
```

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem in ActiveRecord and how do you fix it?
questions.title: The N+1 Query Problem
questions.direct_answer: An N+1 query occurs when code runs one query for a parent collection and then one additional association query for each of its N records. For example, loading posts and calling `post.author.name` in a loop can produce one posts query plus N author queries. `includes`, `preload`, or an appropriate join can fetch the required relationship in a bounded number of queries; the right choice depends on whether the related table is only loaded or also filters the result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can spot N+1 (one query + N per-record queries) and fix it with includes (eager loading).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not noticing the N+1 in the log, or 'fixing' it by caching instead of eager loading.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: N+1 = 1 query for the records + N per-record association queries. Fix with Post.includes(:comments) to eager-load in one extra query.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- N+1 means one collection query followed by one related query per row.
- It often hides inside a view, serializer, or loop that reads an association.
- `includes` or `preload` can load associations in a bounded number of queries.
- Use joins when related columns participate in filtering, with care for duplicate rows.
- Confirm the fix through query logs, tests, strict loading, or profiling—not guesswork.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An N+1 problem starts with one query for a collection and adds one association query for each of its N records. If twenty posts are loaded and a loop lazily reads every `post.author`, the page can run one posts query plus twenty author queries. Database round trips grow with the collection size.

The controller query may look harmless because the extra work begins later in a view or serializer. The first read of each unloaded association asks the database for that record's author. Query caching can hide a few duplicates, but it does not turn this growing access pattern into a reliable bounded plan.

Use `Post.includes(:author)` when the response will read authors and Rails may choose separate queries or a join as needed. `preload(:author)` explicitly uses separate association queries, while `eager_load(:author)` uses a left outer join. Each changes the loading plan before the loop starts.

Use `joins(:author)` when author columns decide which posts SQL should return. A join alone does not promise that later `post.author` reads are preloaded, so a filtered result may use `joins(:author).preload(:author)`. Joined collections can also duplicate parent rows and complicate pagination, especially with has-many relations.

Do not eager-load every association by habit; unused rows and wide joins cost memory and transfer time. Check the actual view or serializer, then confirm the fix in query logs, a query-count test, strict loading, or profiling. The goal is a small bounded query plan that loads only what the response uses.

sections.title: Association laziness turns an innocent loop into repeated I/O
sections.content:
A relation can load the parent rows without loading any association. Each association proxy remembers whether its target is loaded. The first read of an unloaded `post.author` asks the database for that one post's key; repeating the read for different posts repeats the round trip.

Preloading collects keys from all parents and fetches matching children together, then assigns each child to its owner in memory. This changes the number of trips from a value proportional to N to a small bounded number, often two for one association.

Join-based loading solves a different shape. It lets SQL filter or order by related columns, but parent data may be duplicated once per child row and pagination can become subtle. Separate preloading avoids row multiplication, while a join may be necessary for the actual predicate.

Detection belongs near the rendered access path. A controller query can look harmless until a serializer asks for two nested associations. Development logs, Bullet-like tooling, strict loading, and request-level query assertions reveal the real boundary and protect it during later view changes.

sections.title: Complete Rails example: return recent posts with author names
sections.content:
```ruby
class RecentPosts
  def self.with_author_names(limit: 20)
    Post.includes(:author)
        .order(created_at: :desc)
        .limit(limit)
        .map do |post|
          { title: post.title, author: post.author.name }
        end
  end
end

rows = RecentPosts.with_author_names(limit: 2)
rows.each { |row| puts "#{row[:title]} — #{row[:author]}" }
```
